Bianca appeared in the doorway with the indemnity forms Ms. Sato needed signed for the competition travel, watched the arm complete a cycle, and said nothing until Kelvin went to find his pen. Then she said, "He's not going to thank you, you know. He thinks it was half his fix."

"It was half his fix."

"There's the twist, though." She set the forms on the bench. "He asked me in September to tell him if he was dragging the team down. He asked me, not you. I told him everything was fine." She shrugged. "You read one chapter of a book and did in one afternoon what I couldn't do in three months, because I was protecting him."

Kelvin came back with the pen, signed, and slid the forms toward Thomas. "Your turn. And Tuesday, when we test the new timing, you're the one taking notes. Out loud this time."

Thomas picked up the pen and signed his name under Kelvin's.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
Justin had been lying to Mr. Zhang for three weeks, and the lie was starting to smell like old strings. He told him he practiced an hour a night, and Mr. Zhang said "good" in that flat way that meant he knew it wasn't true, and then they both pretended the mistake in bar twelve of the waltz was a small accident instead of a habit. Tonight Justin had brought his mother's chromatic tuner, a rectangle of plastic with a needle and a green light, because he'd decided that if he couldn't sound honest he could at least be tuned.

"Play your open A," Mr. Zhang said, folding himself onto the bench beside him. The studio smelled of rosin and the neighbor's curry, and through the wall a toddler was conducting some private catastrophe.

Justin pressed the string. The needle swung, wobbled, and settled. The little screen read 440.

"Now the A at the twelfth fret."

He shifted his hand up the neck, pressed down, and plucked. The tuner caught the note and the number jumped to 880, exactly double, and Justin laughed out loud before he could stop himself. "Wait, it doubled. Same letter, doubled number."

"An octave," Mr. Zhang said. "One octave higher vibrates at exactly twice the frequency." That was all he offered, the way he offered everything, in the smallest possible piece, and then he watched to see what Justin would do with it.

What Justin did was lose twenty minutes to it. He played the A at the fifth fret and then the same shape five frets higher, checking the tuner each time like a slot machine, and twice the pattern held, the numbers pairing off. His theory teacher at school, Mr. Okafor's replacement, the one Justin privately called an ideologue of scales, insisted that theory came before sound, that you memorized the map and then walked the territory. Justin had hated that class for months. But here was the map doing something: the tuner's arithmetic said the same thing his ear had been lazily knowing all along, that the high A was the low A wearing a different coat, and the two ways of hearing it sat down together in his head like strangers discovering they'd grown up on the same street.

"This is the practicing?" Mr. Zhang said, but there was no real edge in it.

"This is the part I'd actually do at home," Justin admitted. He told him then, because the tuner had somehow loosened the bolt. Half an hour some nights, sometimes none, because after his shift at the garden centre his hands felt like borrowed gloves. He'd kept saying an hour because an hour was what a serious person said, and he wanted Mr. Zhang to file him under serious.

Mr. Zhang was quiet long enough that the toddler next door resolved its catastrophe and moved on. "Gurshan," he said finally. "Gurshan told me you stayed two hours after closing last week tuning their beat-up house guitars, just to hear them matched. He said you seemed, what was his word, insouciant about the overtime." He let that hang there, then: "So it is not the instrument you avoid. It is the account keeping."

Justin felt his ears go hot. He thought of Tye, who never practiced anything and played anyway, joyfully, sloppily, dropping into the music room to massacre three chords while Gurshan winced and Justin, in his careful silence, judged him and envied him in equal parts. Tye played like the outcome didn't matter; Justin played like the outcome was a verdict on his whole future, which was exhausting, and which was why he avoided the bench. He had assumed those were the only two options, the clown or the accountant. But the tuner didn't care about either. It just reported the number, twice as high, twice as true, and the string didn't apologize for being one or the other.

"Twenty minutes," Justin said. "Real ones. Every night, and I'll bring the tuner, and you'll know if I'm lying because the intonation will tell on me."

"Thirty," said Mr. Zhang, "and the waltz, bar twelve."

They worked until the lamp buzzed. On the last pass through, bar twelve arrived and Justin's finger landed a hair late and a hair flat, the needle tipping off the green, and Mr. Zhang said nothing at all, which was somehow the loudest thing he'd said all evening. Justin backed up two bars and played it again, watching the number climb, 440, then up where it belonged, doubled and singing above it, clean.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A down payment is the part of a home's price the buyer pays upfront so less must be borrowed; in British usage it is called a deposit.
story:
The notice had been taped to Hailie's door when they came up the stairs, and now it lay flat on the kitchen table between two mugs of tea, its creases still sharp. Laura read it a second time even though she had already read it once in the hallway. The landlord intended to sell the building, and the tenants had ninety days.

"He can just do that?" Laura asked.

"He can do whatever he wants, apparently." Hailie sat down across from her and pulled her laptop toward her, opening it without looking at the notice again. "Mom's at the bank right now. She thinks maybe we buy something. Which is insane, because we don't have money, but she went anyway."

Laura turned her mug in a slow circle on the table. In her own house, money was a subject her parents handled the way other families handled electrical wiring, behind walls, and she had never once thought about what it cost to keep a roof going over anyone. Here, at Hailie's table, with the late sun coming through the curtains and staining everything a jaundiced yellow, the roof itself was the subject.

"Buy what, though?" she said. "A whole apartment?"

"A flat, whatever." Hailie was typing, scrolling through listings. "Mom's been saving since she started at the clinic. She calls it the deposit money, from when we moved in here. She keeps saying it like that's a huge amount."

They heard the key in the lock, then Hailie's mother came in with her coat still buttoned and the wrong expression on her face, somewhere between deflated and stubborn. She dropped a folder of bank paperwork on the counter and put the kettle back on before she said anything.

Laura, trying to be useful, picked up the folder and leafed through the printed pages. There was a summary sheet at the front with boxes for income, for the loan amount, and for something labeled deposit, a number much larger than any renter's deposit Laura had ever heard of. She frowned at it.

"Wait," she said, half to herself. "The deposit on this place was like a month and a half of rent. This number is huge. Is your mom paying that to the bank to, what, hold the apartment?"

Hailie leaned over and looked at the sheet. "That's not the renter's deposit. That's for the purchase." She typed something, read for a moment, and turned the screen so Laura could see it. "It's the part of the home's price the buyer pays upfront, so less has to be borrowed. Here they call it a down payment. The bank guy kept saying deposit and Mom was confused for the same reason you were. In British English it's the same word. Deposit."

Laura stared at the number again and felt the two meanings slide apart in her head, the small sum locked away against damage, and this other thing, this chunk of the actual price, money that meant you owned a piece of the flat before you even moved in. The tea Hailie's mother set down in front of her had gone lukewarm already, and she drank it anyway.

"What did the adviser say?" Hailie asked her mother.

"That they'd have to underwrite it, all of it, income, the loan, everything, before they decide." Her mother sat down heavily and pushed the folder away an inch, as though it were something that might bite. "Also that ninety days is not very long, which I did not need a professional to tell me."

Nobody spoke for a moment. From the apartment below came the muffled sound of someone practicing phonetics drills, the same vowel repeated with small variations, ah, eh, ih, patient and obsessive, like a person trying to hear the difference between two things that sounded identical.

Laura looked from the folder to the notice to Hailie's face. She had come over intending to help a friend through something, and instead she was sitting in the middle of an education, watching a family try to convert one kind of deposit into another kind, the locked sum unlocked and thrown at a door they wanted to own. She did not know yet whether she thought it was brave or reckless, and she suspected Hailie's mother did not either, and that this was maybe what being an adult was, choosing before you were sure.

"So what happens if the bank says no?" she asked.

"Then we rent somewhere else and Mom loses the money she's been saving for years to fees and moving trucks," Hailie said. "And if they say yes, we spend the next twenty-five years owing more than the flat is worth." She said it flatly, without drama, and closed the laptop. "She's going to do it anyway. She already filled in the forms."

Her mother reached for the pen on the counter and clicked it twice, the way she always did before signing anything, and pulled the summary sheet back toward her. "One of you make more tea," she said.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Canada's federal Goods and Services Tax, introduced on January 1, 1991 at 7 percent, has been 5 percent since January 1, 2008.
story:
Hudson was almost certain he had never made a mistake on a receipt in the four months since the hardware store hired him, which is why he stared at the register tape in his hand like it had insulted his mother. The customer had bought a rake and a coil of garden hose, and the tape showed the subtotal, then a line marked GST at five percent, then the total. He knew the number was right because he rang it himself. What he did not know, until that moment, was that he had never once wondered where the five percent went, or where it came from, or whether five percent had always been five percent. He had a vague feeling it hadn't. He also had a vague feeling his father had told him it had. Both feelings could not be true, and Hudson, being Hudson, decided his father's version was the reliable one.

The next morning was the personal finance unit in Ms. Dang's business classroom, a room he liked for its smell of whiteboard marker and its wall of posters about compound interest that nobody read. Ms. Dang had told them to bring a paycheque stub or a receipt from a part-time job, and Hudson had brought both, folded together in his back pocket like evidence. Amalia slid into the seat beside him with her own stub from the bakery, and Bethany arrived late, as always, holding a coffee she had absolutely not purchased in the cafeteria.

"Alright," Ms. Dang said, "put your documents on the desk. Before I say anything, tell me what you notice." She had a way of asking questions she plainly knew the answers to, which Hudson found either Socratic or lazy, depending on the day.

He laid out the receipt first. "Five percent GST," he said. "It's been five percent forever. My dad said when he was my age it was the same."

Bethany leaned over, sipping her coffee. "It hasn't."

"It has," Hudson said, with the calm of a man who had never been wrong about anything except the capital of Australia, which he still maintained was Sydney.

Bethany already had her phone out, thumb moving with the fluency of someone raised on argument. "Goods and Services Tax," she read. "It came in on January first, nineteen ninety-one, at seven percent. It's been five percent since January first, two thousand eight." She set the phone down between them like a card she'd been holding all morning.

Hudson looked at the receipt, then at the phone, then at Amalia, who was studying her pay stub and pretending very hard not to have heard any of it. Nineteen ninety-one. His father would have been eleven. Hudson tried to metabolize this, the fact that a number he'd treated as permanent had changed within his own father's lifetime, that a percentage could be as revisable as a hem. He'd assumed the tax system was a kind of technocracy, a machine run by experts who set the gears once and let them turn. If the gears could be adjusted, then somebody had their hand on them, and that somebody was not a machine.

"So my dad's wrong," he said slowly.

"Your dad was probably rounding up his own childhood to five," Bethany said. "People do that."

"He does that." Hudson picked up his pay stub next, the little paper rectangle that had baffled him the first time it arrived. He'd worked thirty-one hours and earned a figure he'd already spent in his head, and then the stub subtracted things: federal income tax, CPP, EI, abbreviations that looked like a puzzle in a language he'd never been offered. The money that reached his bank account was less, always less, and until today he had regarded the difference as a kind of weather, unavoidable and not worth discussing. Now he turned the stub over as though the back might have reasons on it. The GST on the rake was a tax on what he spent. The lines on the stub were taxes and deductions on what he earned. Two directions, money leaving him at both ends, and he had simply accepted it the way he accepted gravity.

At lunch they sat on the steps outside the business classroom, and Amalia split a wedge of her epicurean lunch, some cheese and fig thing her mother packed, into three pieces without being asked. "So what did you decide?" she said. "Bethany proved your dad wrong, you proved the government is run by people, is there a conclusion here or are we just admiring the problem?"

"I don't know yet," Hudson said. He held up the receipt, the GST line still legible under his thumb. "It's five now and it was seven and before ninety-one it was nothing, I guess. I mean, probably nothing. I haven't checked that part."

"You haven't checked that part," Bethany repeated, delighted.

"I haven't checked that part," Hudson agreed. He folded the receipt along its old crease and put it back in his pocket, next to the pay stub he'd been meaning to ask his father about all along, and had, it now occurred to him, been avoiding.

"Ask him tonight," Amalia said. "Film it."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
Mr. Chanthavong kept the sign-up sheet on his desk for three days before Kyle wrote his name on it. Peer health educators, the flyer said, would be trained to explain consent, contraception and testing to younger students, and Kyle had told himself it would look good on applications, which was partly true and partly a way of admitting he wanted to do it without saying why. Elly had signed up first, which made it easier. Jay had not signed up at all, and had made that clear.

"You're going to stand in front of ninth graders and talk about condoms," Jay said at lunch, tearing the crust off his sandwich. "Voluntarily."

"Somebody has to," Kyle said.

"Somebody does have to. That's the extenuating part, I guess. If it were nobody's job, it'd be sad. Since somebody's doing it, I just have to be glad it isn't me." Jay said it lightly, but Kyle had noticed that Jay had gone quiet two weeks earlier when a rumor moved through their grade about a girl in the year above, something about a clinic visit, something nobody could verify and everybody repeated anyway.

The training ran on Thursdays after school in the health classroom. Mr. Chanthavong was careful in a way Kyle hadn't expected. He never lectured longer than ten minutes. Consent, he said, was the one topic they could not afford to get wrong, and so they would practice saying it wrong before they practiced saying it right. "You hold a kind of trust here," he told them. "Not a fiduciary duty, nothing so formal as that, but the younger kids will believe you because you're older, and you have to deserve the believing." Kyle wrote that down. When Elly gave her practice run on consent, she kept sliding into a tangential story about a party from eighth grade that didn't actually illustrate anything, and Mr. Chanthavong let her finish before pointing out that a story which proved nothing was worse than no story, because it used up attention. Kyle learned more from watching that than from any of the handouts.

The contraception unit ended with a field trip to the clinic on Miller Street, the one by the pharmacy with the flickering sign. Jay came along, unannounced, hands in his pockets, saying he was bored and had nothing else to do. Inside, the waiting room smelled like disinfective and old magazines, and a rack of pamphlets stood beside the vending machine. While Elly sat with the nurse at the counter comparing options, comparing pill packets to brochures to a small plastic model on the desk, Kyle read the pamphlets, mostly to have something to do with his hands. One of them laid out all the methods on a grid, with the failure rates printed in a column he had to read twice.

The pill, the shot, the condom, each had a number attached, and then two rows near the bottom had numbers so small he checked the footnote to see if the printing was a mistake. Fewer than 1 in 100 users a year. Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants. He leaned toward the counter, where Elly was asking the nurse why anyone would choose the pill if these existed.

"Because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on daily use," the nurse said, turning the brochure toward Elly and tapping the column. "No remembering, no pharmacy refill, nothing you have to do every day."

Kyle looked at Jay, who was staring at a poster about chlamydia with the particular stillness of someone trying to look casual. "So the failure rate is the human rate," Kyle said, mostly to himself. "The pill doesn't fail. People taking the pill fail." The nurse didn't confirm or deny it; she just went back to her checklist of questions for Elly, and Kyle stood there holding the fact, turning it over.

"You should get tested," Kyle said to Jay in the parking lot afterward, quiet enough that Elly wouldn't hear through the glass. "Since we're here. It's a swab and a urine cup. Fifteen minutes."

"I didn't say anything about me."

"I know. You didn't have to."

Jay looked at the door for a long time, then at the pamphlet Kyle was still holding, then went back inside without a word. Kyle waited on the bench by the pharmacy, and Elly came out and sat beside him and asked what that had been about, and Kyle said he wasn't sure yet, which was true.

On presentation day, Kyle stood in front of a ninth grade class with a bowl of wrapped condoms and a diagram of the clinic's hours, and a boy in the second row asked whether the implant really worked for years. Kyle said fewer than 1 in 100 users a year get pregnant on it, same for the hormonal IUD, because once it's placed you don't have to do anything daily, and then he added, "The part nobody can promise you is the remembering, if you pick something else. That part is yours." A girl near the window raised her hand and asked how you bring any of it up with someone you like without it being weird, and Kyle stood there for a second, then said he was still working on that one himself, and wrote it on the board under a heading that said QUESTIONS WE'LL COME BACK TO.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
Ryan's grandmother kept her violin in the front room closet, behind the winter coats, and for the first sixteen years of his life he had walked past that closet without once wondering what was in it. Then, in March, she took it out to tune it for a neighbour's funeral, and Ryan heard the open strings ring against the parlour's high ceiling, and he asked if he could learn. She said he could, on one condition, that he practise in her house and not his parents', because his mother would make it a chore and she refused to watch that happen.

So every Saturday he took two buses to her street of narrow brick houses and sat on the piano bench with the instrument wedged under his chin, sawing at "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" from a beginner's book she had bought used. He was good at reading. He had sung in the school choir since grade seven and the dots on the staff made sense to him the way spelling did, a code you decoded, and he advanced quickly through the book, three pages a Saturday, four. His grandmother sat in her armchair with her tea and her crossword and said only "again" when he rushed, which was often.

The problem arrived in April, wearing a purple backpack. Patience, a girl from his chemistry class, had heard about the Saturday lessons, and her little cousin Samy, who was nine, also played violin, and would Grandma mind if Samy used the front room for half an hour since his own teacher had moved away? Grandma acceded immediately, because she believed a house with one violin learner should have two, the way a house with one cat should have two, and Ryan understood this logic even if he could not defend it.

Samy set up in the corner, and Ryan, packing up, heard him play. Not "Twinkle." Samy played a Vivaldi movement, fast, with slurs and double stops, the whole thing flowing out of him like he was reciting a poem from memory. Ryan stood in the doorway with his beginner's book still in his hand and felt the specific humiliation of a fourteen-year-old who has just watched a nine-year-old do easily what he cannot do at all. Then Samy stopped, and Ryan, trying to be gracious, held out the book and said, "Do you want to try a piece from this? Sight-reading's good practice."

Samy looked at the page the way Ryan's grandmother looked at a crossword clue she didn't know, politely, without recognition. "I can't read the notes," he said. "I play from remembering." He hummed two bars of the Vivaldi to demonstrate, then hummed a fiddle tune Ryan didn't know, then, without warning, the theme from a cartoon Ryan did know, ornamented with three little turns Samy had invented himself. He was, Ryan thought, a connoisseur of his own ears. He could play anything he had heard enough times, and he could not play a single note off a page.

"It's the Suzuki method," Patience said later, on the bus home, when Ryan described it. "Samy's old teacher did it. Shinichi Suzuki, the Japanese violinist, started it. Kids learn to play by ear before they read music, the same way they learn to talk before they learn to read." Ryan said, "Nobody talked to me about reading when I was two," and Patience said, "Exactly," and they rode three stops in silence while Ryan's doctrinaire little soul, which had always believed that notes were the serious way and ears were the party trick, quietly reorganized itself.

He remembered, on the fifth stop, the choir in grade seven, before he could read music at all. Mr. Carvalho had taught them the bass line of an African folk song by call and response, sing it back, sing it back, until the line lived in their throats, and only afterwards put the sheet in front of them, and Ryan had learned it faster than any page he'd decoded since. He had forgotten that, filed it away as a game they'd played before the real work started.

The next Saturday he brought his phone. He recorded his grandmother playing one of her own pieces, a slow Portuguese tune her father had played, and for the whole lesson he put the book away and tried to copy the recording phrase by phrase, getting it wrong, rewinding, getting it less wrong. It felt like groping in a dark room for a light switch he couldn't locate, and when he finally landed the second phrase, his grandmother set down her crossword. "Again," she said, but she said it differently.

Ryan did not stop reading music, and he did not become Samy, and he was honest with himself about both of those things on the bus home, chin against the window, the case between his knees. What he decided, provisionally, without knowing if it would hold, was that he would learn each piece twice, once through his ears and once through his eyes, and see which version told him more, and whether they argued. Patience texted him a picture of Samy holding the beginner's book upside down, squinting at it with tremendous suspicion, and Ryan laughed out loud on the bus, then closed his eyes and played the Portuguese tune in his head, all the way to the second phrase, and then past it.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, the usual North American graduation processional, premiered in 1901 in Liverpool.
story:
The folding chairs in the gymnasium had been arranged in rows so straight they looked rehearsed, and John stood at the end of the far row with his gown half zipped, holding a folded piece of paper he had rewritten four times. Mr. Okonkwo found him there ten minutes before the processional was due to start.

"Hailee has the flu," Mr. Okonkwo said. "Fever since last night. She's not walking. You're second on the list, so the speech is yours if you want it."

John had written a speech anyway, the way you write letters you never send, and now the letter had been asked for. The problem was that he had written it twice, in two moods. One draft argued that the class should be proud of what it had survived; the other argued that pride was cheap and the honest thing was to admit how little any of them knew yet. He had never managed to make the drafts agree with each other, and now he had perhaps eight minutes to decide which version of himself would stand at the podium.

"Can I think while we line up?" he said.

"You can think while you hum," said Blair, who was already in the staging area by the equipment room, straightening her collar with the particular mannerism of someone who touches her collar when she is nervous and knows it and does it anyway. She was humming the processional, the one everyone knows without knowing its name, the tune that means folding chairs and someone's grandmother crying.

"What is that, actually?" John asked. "Does it have a name, or is it just graduation music?"

"Elgar," Blair said. "Pomp and Circumstance, the first one. March Number One."

"Elgar," John repeated, as if filing it. He had assumed the music was as old and anonymous as the ceremony itself, invented by nobody, sprung from the floor of every gymnasium in North America. That it had a composer, a specific person with a name, struck him as oddly hopeful. Even the things that feel permanent were made by somebody, once.

Mr. Okonkwo, checking the line, glanced over. "Premiered in Liverpool," he said. "Nineteen oh one. Look it up, it's true," and he moved on down the row, tapping shoulders, straightening a tassel here and there. He had a way of dropping a fact and leaving, so the fact sat with you like a handed object you were now responsible for.

John turned it over while the line began to move. Nineteen oh one, Liverpool. Blair had said "the first one," which meant there were others, which meant the man had kept going, marching on through variations of his own idea. And the tune had crossed an ocean and a century and attached itself to gymnasiums like this one, to fluorescent light and a smell of floor wax, to kids who thought it had always existed. That was a tangential thought, he knew, standing there in line, but it did the thing he needed done. His two drafts were not enemies. They were the same march in different arrangements. You could be proud and uncertain at once; the pride could even be about the uncertainty, the fact of having gotten this far without a map.

The double doors opened. The music itself, recorded and slightly too loud, came from speakers bolted to the wall, and the line moved forward into the light and the rows of faces. John walked with the paper in his left hand, and when the row of chairs for the graduates was nearly full and Mr. Okonkwo caught his eye and tilted his head toward the podium, John stood up and unfolded both drafts stacked together, the proud one and the honest one, because there was no time left to choose and maybe no need to choose.

"Hailee was supposed to give this speech," he said, "so anything good in it is hers, and the rest is mine." A ripple of tired laughter from the crowd. He told them about Liverpool, nineteen oh one, a composer named Elgar, and the strange life of a tune that gets used for things its writer never imagined. "We're a bit like that," he said. "Somebody wrote the beginning of us, and now we're off in directions nobody planned, and we get to decide what we're for." He did not claim to know what came next. He said he was certain of exactly two things: that they had made it, and that making it was not the same as knowing where they were going. Then he sat down, and the principal called the names, one after another, and when Blair crossed the stage she found him in the second row and touched her collar once, and smiled.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A necessary condition must hold for something to happen but may not be enough: the sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight, but not sufficient, since something may cast a shadow.
story:
Hunter kept the envelope under his thigh on the chair so Deanna wouldn't see it, though she had already spotted it, because Deanna missed nothing.

The coffee shop near campus had gone quiet after the afternoon rush, and the three of them had the table by the window where the light came through hard and flat. Ronin was arguing with Deanna about the early admission list, which had gone up that morning on the university's site, a plain alphabetical page that had ruined several people's week and improved a few others'.

"I'm telling you," Ronin said, tapping his cup, "if you get straight A's, you're in. That's the whole game. Grades are the key."

"That's a colloquialism, not an argument," Deanna said. "A key actually opens the door by itself. Grades don't."

"Then what's the point of them?"

She turned her spoon over on the saucer, thinking. Hunter watched her do it, the way she lined the handle up with the table edge, and he understood she was assembling something.

"Okay. Think about the sun," she said. "The sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight. But it's not sufficient. You can have the sun up and still be standing in a shadow."

Ronin frowned. "Because a building's in the way."

"Right. So the sun is necessary, but it's not enough on its own. Necessary and sufficient are different things. Your grades are like the sun. Without them you don't get direct light. With them, you might still be in the shade."

Hunter's hand went to the envelope. The paper was warm from his leg, and he had not opened it since it arrived, three days ago, in the mailbox with his name printed in a font that looked vaguely official and vaguely like a court summons.

The deadline was tonight. Replies to the early admission offer, if there was an offer, were due by eleven fifty-nine, and it was already past six. He had come here intending to open it in front of them, because he'd decided that opening it alone in his room would be worse, and because Deanna would tell him the truth no matter what it said, and because Ronin would make a joke no matter what it said, and he needed both.

"Here's the thing," Ronin said, leaning back. "Say Hunter got rejected. You'd say, well, his grades were fine but something else was in the way. Fine. But then nothing is ever sufficient, and the word stops meaning anything."

"That's not what the word means," Deanna said. "If grades guaranteed admission, then every single person with straight A's would be in. Every one. One counterexample breaks it."

"And if they were sufficient, they'd also be necessary in reverse," Hunter said, surprising himself. Both of them looked at him. He hadn't planned to speak. "No, wait, that's the part that's not true. The sun has to be up for direct sunlight, but the sun being up doesn't mean you get sunlight. Something can cast a shadow. And I bet the reverse is the same at the university. They take people without perfect grades. So grades might be neither necessary nor sufficient, or necessary but not sufficient, or, I don't actually know which."

The room seemed to slow down around the table. Someone at the counter dropped a ceramic lid and it rang against the floor and rolled, and nobody moved to pick it up. Deanna was watching Hunter's hand, which had moved again to the envelope, and this time she didn't pretend she hadn't seen it.

"Is that it?" she asked quietly.

"It came Tuesday," Hunter said. "I couldn't open it."

Ronin said nothing, which for Ronin was tectonic, a whole personality shifting and going still.

"If I open it and it's a no, then we know my grades weren't sufficient, but we don't know whether they were necessary, because there could be someone with worse grades who got in, and I'd never see that list." He heard himself talking faster, the conditional branching out in front of him like the hallway of a building he was walking through in the dark. "And if it's a yes, that doesn't prove anything either. One case. You can't build a rule out of one case."

"Open it," Deanna said.

He turned the envelope over. The flap was tucked, not sealed, which somehow made it worse, a decision that could be undone, that had never fully been made. Ronin pulled out his phone and put it face down on the table without being asked, which meant he was timing it, which meant it was past six thirty.

Hunter slid his thumb under the flap. The paper inside was one sheet, folded in thirds, and he could see through the back of it that there was not much text, and his whole body understood at once that the moment had come and gone, that whatever the words said had been true since Tuesday and would remain true after tonight; only his knowledge of it was on a deadline.

He unfolded it and read the first line, and then the second, and then he looked up, and Deanna said, "Well?"

"Deferred," he said. "They put me in the regular pool."

Ronin exhaled. "So it's not a no."

"It's not a yes, either." Hunter set the letter on the table between them, in the flat window light, where the shadow of his own cup fell across the corner of the page. "The sun's up," he said. "I just don't know yet what's in the way."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A poll's stated margin of error applies to each candidate's share; the margin of error for the lead between two candidates is about twice as large.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and old popcorn, and the folding tables had been arranged into rows with taped arrows guiding voters toward the check-in desk where Sophia sat with a clipboard. She was too young to vote, seventeen for three more weeks, but Mr. Sánchez, who taught her statistics elective, had arranged for her and two classmates to observe the process and transcribe the turnout counts every hour, by hand, onto a sheet that would go to the county office at noon. She liked the task more than she had expected to. The numbers felt solid in a morning that otherwise kept shifting: the light through the high windows, the shuffle of canes, the evanescent steam off the coffee the poll workers kept pouring for the old man who arrived at six and still hadn't left.

Lana arrived at nine with her phone out. "Four-point lead," she said, dropping into the folding chair beside Sophia and tilting the screen toward her. "Latest poll. Margin of error is three points. So that's it, right? Four is bigger than three. It's basically over."

Sophia looked at the numbers the way Mr. Sánchez had trained them to, before writing anything. Three weeks ago she would have agreed without thinking. She had spent the whole summer doing exactly that, arguing with her father at the kitchen table, waving polls at him like receipts. He had listened with a patience that now embarrassed her to remember, and she had mistaken it for concession.

"It's not the same thing," she said slowly, and Lana's eyebrows went up, waiting. Sophia turned the clipboard over, as if the blank back might help her. She had gotten this wrong on a quiz in September. She'd written that a four-point lead with a three-point margin of error was outside the error, therefore safe, and Mr. Sánchez had circled it in red and written only, ask yourself whose error. She had stared at that note for two evenings before it opened. The three points, she'd realized, wrapped around each candidate's own share. The lead sat between them, and error on two wobbly things leaning on each other didn't stay the same size. The margin of error for the lead was about twice as large. Six points, not three. And four lived comfortably inside six.

"Say that again," Lana said, in the flat voice she used when she suspected she was being managed.

"The three points is for each candidate's number," Sophia said. "The gap between them? That's about double. Six. So a four-point lead could actually be a two-point deficit, and the poll would still be doing its job perfectly."

Lana pulled the phone back and looked at it as though it had lied to her personally. "That's a terrible way to design a poll."

"It's not designed," Sophia said. "It's just how it works."

Mr. Sánchez came over with the nine o'clock count sheet, and his eyes moved between them. He didn't ask what they'd been discussing, which Sophia appreciated; she remembered, with a small flinch, the quiz, and how she'd gone up to his desk after class to argue and left having conceded everything. "Phylogeny," he said instead, tapping the laminated poster on the gym wall, one of several from the science fair still taped up along the bleachers, a branching tree of some beetle family rendered in green ink. "Somebody's project. Odd thing to have behind a voting booth." He took the count sheet and moved on toward the check-in table.

Lana was quiet for a while after that. The line of voters thickened as mid-morning arrived, parents with strollers, a woman with a guide dog whose nails clicked on the varnished floor, a man who argued pleasantly with the poll worker about whether he'd moved precincts. Sophia copied the tally marks onto the official sheet, transcribing each cluster of five carefully, because an error here would propagate, a word she'd learned the same week as the margin of error and liked less every time she used it.

"So what you're saying," Lana said finally, "is nobody knows anything."

"No." Sophia pressed the pen down, thinking. "It's more like, the poll knows exactly as much as it says and we keep reading it as more." She thought of her father again, and of the summer, and how certainty had felt so much better than this, like standing on a floor instead of a raft. She still wasn't sure she preferred the raft. "Four points is still a lead. It's just not a locked door."

"That's a terrible slogan."

"I know."

A poll worker called the ten o'clock hour, and Sophia stood to walk the rows and count heads, as she'd been shown, touching each folded booth with her eyes in turn. Behind her, Lana had picked up her phone again, but she wasn't reading the number at the top this time; she was scrolling, frowning, hunting for the smaller print underneath it.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In Westminster-style parliaments, the third reading is the final debate and vote on a bill as amended, after its details have been examined in committee.
story:
The folding tables of the school hall had been arranged into a horseshoe, and Brandon sat inside it with his motion folder squared on his knees, the way he had seen the real members do on television. He had drafted the bill himself in October, a plain clause about later school start times, printed it, given copies to Kingsley and Kenley, and watched it survive first reading on a show-of-hands vote that nobody really contested. Then committee had taken it apart. The clause that set the start time at nine had been amended to "encourage consultation," and the word "shall" had become "may," and the paper in his folder now said something weaker than the paper he had written.

"You're going to speak against your own bill," Kingsley said beside him, not quite a question. Kingsley had argued in committee for the amendment, politely, the way he argued everything, and afterward had come to Brandon's locker to explain that half a law was better than a law that failed. He proselytized about compromise the way other people proselytized about bands, sure and cheerful and impossible to shake off.

"Or for it," Brandon said. "I haven't decided."

Mr. Tse, who taught civics and acted as Clerk for the model parliament, stood at the little table by the window and read out the order paper. The afternoon light came through the tall panes and lay across the linoleum in pale rectangles, and a fly kept landing on the water jug. "Order. Second item. Third reading of Bill Four, the school start times bill, as amended in committee." He looked up over his glasses at Brandon. "The third reading is the final debate and vote on the bill as amended. Member for Ashford, you have the floor."

Brandon stood. Two nights ago he had wanted to condemn the amendment, to call it a gutting, and he had written a speech that did exactly that, full of the word "betrayal." He had read it aloud in his bedroom and heard how it sounded, how much of it was for the sound of itself, and he had torn the pages in half. The version in his hand now began differently.

"Mr. Speaker, I wrote this bill because I watched my sister fall asleep over her homework every night for three years. The committee took out the part that would have fixed that. I'm not going to pretend it didn't." He heard chairs shift, and made himself go on. "But the bill as amended still requires the school to consult, to gather the evidence, to put the question in writing. That's the ground the next bill stands on. I'd rather hold a small piece of solid ground than a large piece of nothing." He sat down before his voice could do anything theatrical.

Kenley rose in her seat across the horseshoe. She had voted against the amendment in committee and had told Brandon at lunch that she thought accepting it made him an egoist, more attached to being the bill's author than to its purpose. She had said it while eating fries, and it had stung more than she probably meant it to. Now she folded her arms. "A point," she said. "If we pass this as amended, we're telling everyone the problem is solved. Nobody drafts the next bill. I've watched it happen with the recycling motion last year."

"That's a risk," Brandon said, and he was surprised to find he meant the words, that they were not just a concession he had rehearsed. "But the vote today is on this text, not on the one we wish existed. If it fails, there's no consultation and no next bill either. There's just the timetable we have now."

The debate ran another twenty minutes. A member from the back benches compared the amendment process to igneous rock, something that had been melted down and cooled into a harder shape than it started as, and Kingsley said that was the first intelligent thing anyone had said all afternoon. Then Mr. Tse called the division, and they filed through the lobby doors to be counted, the way the real parliament did, the Clerk's pencil ticking names. Brandon walked through the aye lobby with his heart going hard against his ribs, and through the glass panel in the door he watched Kenley hesitate between the two lobbies for a long second before she turned and followed him.

The count was forty-one to nineteen. Mr. Tse announced the result, recorded the assent of the model Governor General, a tired student in a borrowed blazer who signed the paper with a flourish, and declared that Bill Four had passed into law, such law as a model parliament could make. The hall broke into the rustle of closing folders and scraped chairs.

Kenley caught up with him at the door, bag over her shoulder. "I still think we capped it too low," she said. "I changed my vote because you changed your argument, not because you were right."

"I know," Brandon said. "I'm not sure I was right either. Ask me in a year, when we see whether anyone actually consults." He held the door for her, and outside the sky had gone the flat grey of late afternoon, and the bill, the weaker, harder version of it, was folded into his folder under his arm.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Brody stood in the middle of the living room with his phone against his ear, his voice bouncing off bare drywall, and Kiley said, "Say it again, you're echoing."

"I said the movers come tomorrow and we're sleeping here tonight. Air mattresses." He turned in a slow circle. There was no furniture to interrupt the sound, nothing on the counters, a single bulb burning in the ceiling of the kitchen. "It's like being inside a shoebox that hasn't been assigned a foot yet."

Kiley laughed, then stopped laughing, and the silence on the line had a texture to it, like she was holding something behind her teeth. Three hundred miles, his father kept saying, as though the number were small because the road between was straight.

Nathanael showed up around six with two grocery bags, which was ridiculous, because there was no table, no plates, no fridge with power yet. "Hot dogs," he announced. "Mr. Wardak said we could use his grill. He's the neighbor on the left, the one with the garden."

Mr. Wardak turned out to be a retired science teacher with careful hands and a grill older than any of them. He lit the coals without hurry, asked Nathanael to hold the lid, and set out a folding chair for Kiley's mother, who had driven her over and stayed to say a proper goodbye. Brody noticed that Mr. Wardak kept a bowl of water by the gate for dogs that were not his, and that he repositioned it twice as the shade moved.

They ate standing up, balancing plates on their knees in the empty living room, headlamps on because the overhead light in that room didn't work yet. Kiley said, "Okay, I've been avoiding this all day. Ninety hours. Have you actually done the math?"

"What math?"

"The study you told us about last month. The Jeffrey Hall one, 2018. You said it takes about ninety hours together to go from casual friend to friend." She pulled her knees up onto the air mattress. "You and Nathanael, you're already way past that. You and me, way past. But the people at the new school, they start at zero. You're going to be a transfer with no banked time."

Brody set his plate down on the floor. He had read the study during a bored afternoon in the library and mentioned it once, mostly because it had felt like trivia, and now Kiley was turning it over like a stone with something underneath. "So what, I clock in? I hand people a punch card?"

"I'm saying it's not instant," Kiley said. "So don't decide by October that everybody there hates you. It's just that nobody's put in the hours yet."

Nathanael, who had been quiet in the way he got when he was working out whether to say a thing, said, "There's another side of it, though. Ninety hours is like, what, three hours a week for most of a school year. If you sign up for stuff, if you show up to the same room every week, the hours just happen. It's not a worse place. It's just earlier."

"Earlier," Brody repeated. He lay back on the air mattress and looked at the ceiling, where the builders had left pencil marks, faint measurements nobody had erased. He had been carrying a story in his head for two weeks, a story in which the move amputated something essential, and it had been easier to hold onto the story than to test it. "I keep imagining the first day as a verdict. Like they'll all decide about me at lunch."

"That's not tenable," Kiley said. "You can't live in a version of the future where you've already lost. I mean it, it doesn't hold up. You'd be doing the deciding for them."

Brody rolled onto his side to look at her. "Since when do you talk like a debate coach?"

"Since I spent four years next to you and Nathanael arguing about everything. I absorbed it, like radiation." She grinned, but her eyes were doing the thing they did when she was about to cry and was determined not to, and Brody reached over and straightened the collar of her jacket, which had gone askew, because he did not know what else to do with his hands.

Nathanael said, "You're going to meet people who act like your friends in the first week, by the way. The ones who latch on because you're new and interesting. Sycophants, basically. And you'll know in your gut they're not real, but it'll feel nice anyway, and you'll be tempted." He shrugged. "Just remember the fake fast ones and the real slow ones look identical at hour ten. The ninety hours is how you tell them apart. That's all the study is good for. It's a patience machine."

Mr. Wardak appeared in the doorway with a pitcher of lemonade and four plastic cups, having apparently decided that the conversational fog rolling out the open front door was his business too. He poured without asking, handed cups around, and said only, "The coals are out. I locked my gate." Then he stood there a moment longer, and Brody saw the old teacher looking at the three of them sprawled across the air mattress, and something in his face suggested he had watched a great many departures and knew exactly what they cost and what they didn't.

"You'll be incapacitated by homesickness for about a month," Nathanael said. "Doc's word, not mine. I looked it up. It's like an injury, it just needs time and you shouldn't walk on it."

"That is the worst comfort anyone has ever given me," Brody said, and Kiley laughed so hard she spilled lemonade on the air mattress, and they all three bent to dab at it with paper towels, kneeling together on the cold new floor of the house where nobody had ever lived, and the clock on the bare wall of the kitchen, the only thing his father had unpacked, ticked steadily toward midnight.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
story:
The book club met on Thursdays in the back room of the library, where the radiators clanked and the window fogged from twelve bodies breathing over cheap cookies. Ashton arrived early because he had an argument to win, or at least to survive. The reading was Jane Eyre, chapters one through ten, and Mr. Pritchard had asked them to try reading the passage where Jane is locked in the red room through "a critical lens," which Ashton had privately decided was a phrase teachers used when they wanted you to be wrong in a more complicated way.

He had prepared two lenses, copied from the school database at eleven the night before. The feminist one asked who was silenced and who was allowed to speak. The Marxist one asked who owned things and who owned nothing. Jane, sent to the red room by her aunt, seemed to fit both: a girl with no money, no property, no defender, screaming at a household that treated her scream as a defect in her rather than a response to its treatment. He had the quotes marked with green sticky notes, and he kept smoothing them flat against his knee.

Sebastian arrived with his copy unread but with a theory about why Brontë had chosen red, a theory involving blood and fire and possibly communism, delivered before his coat was even off. Aedan arrived last, carrying nothing, which was usual. What was not usual was that Aedan had been the one, last week, to ask why so few of the classic novels on their list had been written by women, a question that had landed in the room and stayed there like a smell nobody would name. Ashton suspected Aedan had a real stake in that question, though Aedan never explained his stakes.

The discussion turned to the red room, and Mr. Pritchard, who mostly sat by the cookie plate and said things like "go on," asked them to consider who in the house could abrogate Jane's punishment and why none of them did. Nobody used the word back at him, but the question worked on the room. Bessie could not countermand Mrs. Reed; the servants' obedience was purchased with their wages. Sebastian, surprising everyone, said that Jane was a kind of inventory, a thing Mrs. Reed kept because her late husband had instructed her to, which made her care a fiduciary duty rather than love. Ashton wrote that down, half annoyed that Sebastian had produced something good while so obviously unprepared.

Then Aedan said, quietly, that the problem wasn't just this house. He said his mother had started writing something last year, a memoir, and had stopped, and that the laptop was always in the kitchen where everyone needed it, and there was never a door he could hear close. He said it without looking up, picking chocolate off a cookie he wasn't eating. "It's not like Brontë's time," he said. "But the laptop's still in the kitchen."

Ashton felt his two lenses slide against each other. The Marxist reading said money; the feminist reading said the room. He had been treating them as rival explanations, and now, listening to Aedan and the radiator's capricious knocking, he understood they could be one statement. He remembered something he'd skimmed past at eleven at night: an essay by Virginia Woolf, A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, arguing that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction. Money and a room. Both. He had dismissed it as a thesis statement; now it sounded like the two lenses fused into a single fact about the world.

He said it out loud, carefully, not as a quote but as a thought: that the silence on their reading list and the silence in Jane's red room might have the same architecture, that the gate and the bank account and the closed door were the same wall seen from different sides. Mr. Pritchard asked whether that covered everything. Ashton admitted it didn't. It didn't explain why Mrs. Reed, who had both money and rooms, chose cruelty, or why some women without either had still written. He said he trusted the idea without being able to prove it was complete, and the admission felt less like losing the argument than like setting part of it down.

Sebastian said that was mushy. Aedan said, "No, it's not," and then, still not looking up, asked Mr. Pritchard whether they could choose a woman writer for the next book, and Mr. Pritchard said he thought they could, actually, and reached for the cookie with the most chocolate left on it.

Outside, the fogged window had cleared a narrow stripe at the bottom, and through it Ashton watched the parking lot lights come on one by one, while Aedan wrote something in the margin of Sebastian's unopened copy of Jane Eyre.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
story:
Hayden's father handed him the keys in the parking lot of the registry office, the way someone hands over a live wire, palm open, saying nothing. The car was the old sedan, the one with the dent in the rear door from the mailbox incident three summers ago, when Hayden's mother had misjudged a turn and then laughed about it for a week. His father walked around to the passenger side and got in and folded the map he wasn't going to use.

"You checked the mirrors," his father said. Not a question, so Hayden just adjusted the rearview anyway, tilting it until the parking lot's white lines slid into place. He turned the key. The engine caught on the second try, which his father pretended not to notice, and Hayden eased the car out of the space with the exaggerated care of a man defusing something.

They had waited forty minutes inside the registry office, long enough for Hayden to read every poster on the wall twice while his father filled out forms at the counter. There had been a girl there from his school, Liliana, someone he knew well enough to nod at and not much more, waiting for her permit test with her number crumpled in her fist. She had stood in front of one poster for a long time, arms crossed, and finally said to him, "Did you see this? It says drivers our age, sixteen to nineteen, have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers twenty and older. Per mile. That's per mile, so it's not just that we drive more or less. We're just more likely to die in this thing." She'd looked at the car keys in his hand and then away, and Hayden had wanted to say something reassuring and hadn't been able to think of anything that was also true.

Now, at the first red light, his father said, "Go when it turns. Don't rush the clutch." The light changed and Hayden stalled the car. Behind them, someone honked once, a thin sound that seemed to presage nothing so much as the driver's own impatience, and Hayden restarted and lurched forward and told himself the heat in his face was from the sun through the windshield.

The lesson was supposed to last an hour. Residential streets first, then the bigger road out past the shopping center, then back. Hayden took the corners slowly enough that a jogger passed them twice. His father made small corrections, hand hovering near the wheel, and after the third one Hayden said, "You could just tell me what I'm doing wrong instead of doing the thing with your hand." His father lowered the hand. "You're doing fine," he said, in the voice he used when fine was a kind of reparation for something, though Hayden couldn't name what.

They pulled into the shopping center lot to practice parking, and it was there, wedging the sedan between two minivans on the fourth attempt, that Hayden finally said it. "Liliana's taking her test today too. She was reading this poster at the office. About crash rates." He recited the statistic, got it right, watched his father's face. "Almost three times, for our age. Sixteen to nineteen, compared to twenty and up. Per mile driven." His father was quiet for a moment, checking the space between their bumper and the minivan's. "You can drive well and it's still true," he said. "Both things at once."

Hayden let the car idle. He wanted to argue one side or the other, that the number was a reason to be careful or a reason the whole thing was madness, but neither position felt tenable on its own. The poster didn't say why, and his father didn't know, and Liliana with her crossed arms hadn't known either, and yet the four of them in that office, all the teenagers with their folded numbers, would be on the road by September regardless. He put the car in reverse, straightened the wheel, and eased back into the space, dead center this time, close enough to perfect that he felt a small unfair pride in it.

On the drive home his father told him to take the long way, past the water tower, and Hayden did, signaling early, checking the mirror where the shopping center shrank and then disappeared. Somewhere behind them Liliana was probably still at the office, number called or not called, and the poster was still on the wall telling the same fact to whoever stood in front of it next. The light at the main intersection turned yellow as they approached and Hayden braked smoothly, no lurch, the car settling like something persuaded.

"Again Saturday?" his father asked.

Hayden nodded, and turned the wheel toward home.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Delayed-onset muscle soreness usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it.
story:
Tyson felt fine on Tuesday night, which was the problem. He had pushed through the tryout drills until his lungs burned and his shirt stuck to his back, and then he had walked home under the streetlights feeling like an athlete, like someone whose body had finally been asked a real question and answered it. On Thursday morning he could barely get down the stairs. His thighs seized at every step, and when he lowered himself onto the bus seat he made a sound that made the woman across the aisle look up from her phone.

"Day after tomorrow you'll be worse," Raina said at lunch, not looking up from her own sandwich. "Maybe not worse. Peak."

"Peak?"

"Delayed-onset muscle soreness," she said, and shrugged, as if she were reciting the ingredients on a label. "It hits somewhere between twenty-four and seventy-two hours after you do something your body's not used to. Not right after. Later."

Tyson stared at her. He had assumed, all his life, that pain was a receipt, printed immediately, that you got what you paid for at the register. The idea that a workout could be a debt collected two days later felt almost dishonest. "So Monday's practice is going to land on me Saturday."

"Or Sunday. Or not at all, if you actually warm up." Raina had been playing club ball since she was twelve, and she talked about training the way other people talked about weather, as a system you studied rather than an argument you won.

That was the piece that stung. Tyson had skipped the warm-up on Tuesday because warming up felt like a superstition, something for younger kids and careful adults, and he had wanted to seem like neither. Now he sat in the gym after last period, watching the junior team run layup lines, and spread a notebook on the bleachers. At the far basket Ms. Warsame, who taught geography and opened the gym on Thursdays for anyone who asked, was rebounding for Kaylie, who had cut her foot on a sidewalk grate in August and was only now trusting the floor again.

"You're doing the thing," Kaylie called to him between shots, nodding at the notebook. "The planning thing. Raina told me."

"I'm attempting it."

"Attempt harder. She'll check it, you know. She checked mine."

Tyson wrote Monday at the top of the page and then stopped, pen hovering. His first instinct was six days of drills, everything he could name, stacked like sandbags against a flood. His second instinct was to think about the stairs this morning, how he'd had to lower himself by the handrail like an old man, and to understand, for the first time, that the soreness hadn't been a verdict on his effort. It had been a verdict on his spacing. He had asked for three weeks of change in one afternoon.

Ms. Warsame wandered over during a water break, towel around her neck. In her geography class she had once spent forty minutes dismantling Tyson's confident claim that a theocracy was just a country with a strong leader, drawing the distinction between power that claims divine right and power that merely claims majority, and she regarded his notebook now with the same patient skepticism. "What's Wednesday?" she asked.

"Rest," Tyson said. "Legs, anyway. I'll shoot free throws. Nothing that."

"And Friday?"

"Rest. Full. Then Saturday, light work, because Tuesday's soreness might still be peaking then. It doesn't always clear by then."

She nodded once, which from her was a paragraph. "The players I've watched last past twenty-two are the ones who learned that early," she said, and went back to rebounding, and that was the entire lecture.

The harder question was the one he couldn't schedule around, and he was honest enough to write it in the margin where Kaylie couldn't read it upside down: what if the coach sees rest days as soft? Tyson had grown up in a gym culture where sitting out was a confession, where the whistle had desensitized everyone to the difference between discipline and damage, so that a boy limping through drills was praised and a boy stretching on the sideline was quietly rescheduled. He could plan the perfect week on paper and still face the moment when the plan collided with a coach's raised eyebrow. He didn't know yet what he'd do in that moment. He underlined the margin note twice, which was as close as he could get to an answer.

Kaylie finished her shooting, walked over, and dropped onto the bleacher beside him, unlacing her shoes. "Trade," she said. "You look at my foot schedule, I look at your leg schedule." She read the page slowly, lips moving. "You put the hardest day after the full rest day."

"Is that wrong?"

"It's either genius or a mistake," she said. "We'll find out Monday."

Monday came, and the soreness from Tuesday's tryout had mostly faded by then, which felt like evidence but might have been luck, and Tyson got to the gym twenty minutes early, before anyone could see him and decide what it meant. He started with the warm-up he'd written out word for word on the back of the schedule: ankle circles, hip swings, slow knee bends, then faster. His thighs still muttered but they didn't argue. When Raina pushed through the door with her bag over her shoulder, he was already mid-line of his second set, and she stopped, watched him for a second, and held up her phone with the timer running.

"Two minutes," she said. "Same as the page."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: False friends are words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning; Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed.
story:
The topic for the fifth-minute debate was social media and adolescent mental health, and Chloe had drawn the side arguing that the platforms were harmless, which was not a position she held. She did not mind. Her mother had said once that arguing a side you distrust is how you learn what your own side is worth, and Chloe had filed this away as a truism, the kind of thing adults say that turns out to be true later, when you are standing in Mr. Siddiqui's classroom with index cards sweating soft in your hand.

Everything had to be in Spanish. Five minutes, no English, on a Thursday afternoon in front of the whole class, graded. Chloe had been studying the language for three years, which was enough to read a short story slowly and not enough to think in it, and thinking was the whole point of a debate. She had practiced in the car, in the shower, once to the cat, who had seemed unconvinced.

Luca went first, on the other side. He was fluent in a loud way, all confidence and rolled r's, and he was winning until about minute three, when he leaned forward and declared that teenagers who spent too much time online ended up "embarazadas, vergonzosas, aisladas." The room broke. Half the class laughed, and half looked around to see whether they should. Chloe laughed too, and then caught herself, because she did not actually know why it was funny.

"It means pregnant," Diego whispered to her from the next desk, still grinning. "Embarazada. Not embarrassed. False friends. Looks the same, isn't." He said it the way he said most things, like a gift he could not believe you did not already have. Chloe wrote it on her card, small, in the margin: embarazada = pregnant, NOT embarrassed. A word that looked like a lifeline and was a trapdoor. She thought about how many other words in her speech might be standing there, smiling, wearing a familiar coat.

When her turn came, she stood and looked at Luca's side of the room and abandoned her first card entirely. She had planned to argue that anxiety about social media was overstated, but the argument as she had drafted it was tautological: teens who are fine online are fine, therefore online is fine, which proved nothing and would convince no one. So instead she said, slowly, assembling each sentence like a shelf, that maybe adults had started to pathologize ordinary teenage loneliness, calling every quiet hour a symptom, and that this frightened teenagers more than the phones did. Her grammar wobbled. Twice she stopped, hunting a word, and the silence was enormous, and she let it be enormous rather than reaching for a word that might betray her. When she wanted to say that teens felt ashamed, she said "se sienten avergonzadas," checking the shape of it against her margin note, and the word held.

In the last minute she said something she had not planned, because it arrived in Spanish before it arrived in English: it was possible that both things were true at once, that the phones changed them and that the fear of the phones changed them too, and she did not know yet which weight was heavier. Her time ran out eleven words into that sentence. She sat down with her heart going hard against the desk edge.

Then Mr. Siddiqui, who had been scoring at the back, raised his head and said the twist with a perfectly straight face: "For the record, Luca has won the round, because Chloe, in her final sentence, used 'embarazada' correctly and 'avergonzada' incorrectly, and neither of them means what most of you laughed at." The class went quiet, doing the arithmetic. Luca had used the wrong word and sounded right; Chloe had used the right words and sounded unsure, and the grade had gone to the performance, not the truth.

Afterward, in the corridor, Diego caught up with her. "You know what the worst part is?" he said. "In English I did the same thing last year. Told my cousin her presentation was 'comprehensive.' She'd just asked if it was long." He laughed, then stopped. "It went badly." Chloe looked at her index cards, at the margin note, at the long afternoon ahead, and held them out to him. "Quiz me," she said.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US Fair Labor Standards Act took effect on October 24, 1938, setting the first federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour and a maximum workweek of 44 hours.
story:
The warehouse smelled of cardboard and cold metal, and Mackenzie had learned to like it, the way the shelves rose into shadow like a city with no sky. She was sixteen, three weeks into the job, pulling orders from a scanner that beeped at her like a small, patient nemesis. Today the scanner had routed her past the break room twice, and both times she had heard Lilian's voice getting louder.

"You cannot tell me seven twenty-five is legal," Lilian was saying to Mr. Grant when Mackenzie came in with her water bottle. Lilian was maybe nineteen, worked the loading dock, and had a way of standing with her weight on one hip that made every argument seem already half won. "I checked my hours. Forty-nine last week. Nobody said a word about overtime until I asked."

Mr. Grant, the shift supervisor, had his clipboard against his chest like a shield. "Company policy is straight time until you hit the state threshold," he said. "Take it up with the office."

"The office. Right." Lilian turned and saw Mackenzie hovering in the doorway. "You. You're in school. What do they teach you, anything about this?"

Mackenzie thought of her grandfather, actually, before she thought of school. There was a memory she carried around like a coin in a pocket: the Thanksgiving she was eleven, when he had told the table about his first job, back before the law, when a man could work you sixty hours and pay what he pleased. "Then the Fair Labor Standards Act came," he had said, tapping the tablecloth with two fingers, "October 24, 1938. First federal minimum wage in the country. Twenty-five cents an hour, and they capped the workweek at forty-four hours." Her uncle had whistled and said a quarter wasn't anything, and her grandfather had said it was everything if you'd been getting nothing, and the argument had gone on over the pie while Mackenzie sat quietly doing the math on her napkin.

"It's called the Fair Labor Standards Act," she said now, surprising herself by speaking. "Nineteen thirty-eight. It set the first federal minimum wage at twenty-five cents an hour, and a maximum workweek of forty-four hours."

Lilian stared at her. "Twenty-five cents."

"It was 1938," Mackenzie said. "But it was the first time there was any federal floor at all. My grandpa told me. He said before that, nothing stopped them from working you as long as they wanted."

"October 24, 1938," Lilian said slowly, trying it out. "Twenty-five cents, forty-four hours." She turned back to Mr. Grant, and something in her posture changed, less heat and more spine. "So the whole idea, from the very beginning, was that there's a limit. A legal one. And my question is whether forty-nine hours at straight time fits that idea now."

"That was eighty-seven years ago," Mr. Grant said. "Different world."

"Then there's a newer law," Lilian said. "There's always a newer law. That's the point of the first one."

He wrote something on his clipboard, which was what he did instead of conceding, and walked off toward the dock. Lilian didn't watch him go. She was pulling up something on her phone, a page about the union that represented the warehouse workers two towns over, where the drivers had negotiated their own wage scale and their own overtime rules, separate from what the law required at minimum.

"See, that's the part nobody explains," Lilian said, half to Mackenzie and half to the phone. "The law's a floor. A floor. The union's the part where you build the house on top of it. My aunt did twenty years in a grocery with a contract, and her schedule was posted, actual posted, three weeks out. Meanwhile I find out my hours on Sunday night by text." She laughed without much humor in it. "My aunt also says union dues, and meetings, and a strike in '04 she still has feelings about. So it's not free, is what I'm saying."

Mackenzie turned her water bottle in her hands. At school the words had always come to her parametrized, so to speak, as columns in a textbook: management on one axis, labor on the other, a neat graph you could plot. Standing in the break room with the scanners beeping beyond the wall, the graph would not stay flat. The company paid her legally, probably; Mr. Grant had a clipboard and a mortgage, probably; Lilian had a phone bill and a bad shift schedule she hadn't agreed to. Three true things at once, and none of them cancelled the others out.

"I don't know if a union would fix it," Mackenzie said carefully. "I know the floor exists. That part I'm sure of."

"That's more than the office will tell me," Lilian said. "Twenty-five cents." She said it again, softer, as if tasting the distance between then and now. Then she pocketed her phone, picked up the laminated sheet with the break schedule nailed crookedly above the sink, and pulled it off the wall to read the fine print at the light by the door.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
Kaylee stood at the back of the parish hall holding a bundle of marigolds she had been sent to buy that morning, and she could not make herself walk forward. The altar tables had been pushed together near the window, draped in purple paper, and families were already arranging photographs and plates of food on them. Her mother waved her over with the impatience of someone balancing a tray of pan de muerto and a two-year-old nephew.

"We need the cempasúchil now," her mother said. "Spread them from the door to the altar. The path has to be complete before your abuela's picture goes on."

"Why the door?" Kaylee asked, though she had half known the answer since she was small.

"They call them the guide," her aunt said, not looking up from the sugar skulls she was lining along the table's edge. "The color and the smell lead the souls home."

Later, kneeling on the hall's cold floor while other families stepped around her, Kaylee laid the orange heads in a loose line from the double doors toward the altar. The scent rose thick and green, almost medicinal, and it did something strange to her memory: it returned her, all at once, to her grandmother's kitchen in November, to the same smell rising from a jar of tea her grandmother insisted would cure anything. Kaylee had been eleven the last time she refused to drink it. She had rolled her eyes, said something about the placebo effect she had just learned in science class, and watched her grandmother's face close like a door. Two months later her grandmother was gone, and Kaylee had spent years telling herself the two things were unrelated. Tonight she was less sure, which was itself a kind of unwelcome news.

She was still arranging the flowers when Sarina found her, phone in hand, taking pictures for the school's culture club page. "This is so beautiful," Sarina said. "Okay, dumb question, but do people actually believe the dead come back?"

"That's not a dumb question, it's the only question." Kaylee sat back on her heels. "The marigolds are supposed to guide them. November first and second. That's the whole point of the ofrenda."
