She gestured at the altar her family was building, the framed photograph propped waiting against a candle.

"And you believe it?"

Kaylee looked down the flower path she had almost finished. "I believe my abuela believed it. I believe she thought I was rude the last time I saw her, and I didn't fix it, and now there's a holiday that says I get two more days a year to try." She heard how it sounded, half bitter, half hopeful, and let it stand. "So do I believe the soul literally walks up a row of flowers? No. Do I believe I'm supposed to act like she can still be reached? Tonight, yes."

Sarina lowered her phone. "That's not a contradiction?"

"It might be. I haven't worked it out." Kaylee stood, brushing dust from her knees. "But I know that refusing to find out felt worse than anything. I used to think not believing things was the smart position. Like it protected you. It just made me mean, mostly."

Her cousin Emeric appeared with the photograph, and the whole family gathered while her mother smoothed the cloth and set out a small cup of the tea her grandmother used to make, brewed that afternoon from a recipe nobody had written down. Kaylee's uncle said a few words in Spanish that she caught only in pieces. Her mother lifted the frame and paused, waiting, and Kaylee understood that the pause was for her, that everyone remembered that last afternoon even if no one had ever named it.

She took the photograph from her mother's hands. It was heavier than she expected, or her arms were tired from the flowers, and she stood a moment with her grandmother's nineteen-year-old face looking out at her from a wedding day decades before Kaylee was born. "I'm sorry about the tea," she said quietly, to the photo, to the room, to whatever might or might not be listening. Then she placed it on the ofrenda, centering it between the candles, and stepped back into her mother's arm around her shoulders.

Outside the hall doors, the November air had gone torpid and heavy for the season, holding the last warmth of an afternoon that didn't want to end. Mr. Yilmaz, the neighbor from across the street who had come to observe the community celebration, was reading the small printed sign about the altar, and he asked Kaylee, as she passed, whether the families truly left the marigolds out overnight. She told him they left everything out, food and flowers and all, for the visiting dead. He nodded slowly and did not ask his next question, and Kaylee walked back inside to where her family sat sharing the bread, one cup of tea steaming untouched beside her grandmother's photograph.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Electric field strength can be measured in volts per metre or in newtons per coulomb, and the two units are equivalent.
story:
The skate park emptied toward dusk, and Anais spread her physics worksheet on the flat bottom of a quarter pipe, weighting the pages with a wax candle and her helmet. Between two charged plates, the problem said, find the field strength at a point midway. She had copied her diagram twice already, once at school and once here, because the first version had wobbled into something she no longer trusted. Above her a boarder carved the shallow end in long, patient arcs, and she noticed, not for the first time, how the curved wall slowed him the way a hill slows a bicycle, invisibly and by degrees.

She was still staring at her own numbers when Yannick dropped onto the concrete beside her, board clattering, and Rayan followed, shaking gravel from his cuffs. Neither of them had done the homework. Both of them had opinions about it anyway. Yannick borrowed her pencil without asking and worked the midpoint calculation in a quick, confident hand, then turned the page toward her as though presenting evidence. "Four thousand," he said. "Volts per metre. That's the field strength."

Rayan, saturnine in the fading light, took the pencil next and did the same arithmetic differently, or so it appeared, arriving at four thousand newtons per coulomb. He tapped the figure twice. "Force per unit charge. That's what an electric field is. Mine's the real quantity. His is just some voltage thing."

They argued for a while, and Anais listened with the particular attention she paid to arguments where both people seemed right. Yannick said volts per metre; Rayan said newtons per coulomb; the number under both was the same, four thousand, and neither of them seemed to have noticed that coincidence, or if they had, they'd dismissed it as luck. She wondered whether it was luck. She wondered whether two honest measurements of one thing could wear different clothes and still be the same body.

She took the worksheet back and drew a small bracket around each unit, a habit of hers, delimiting the parts of a problem she didn't yet understand so she could look at them separately. Volts per metre. Newtons per coulomb. She said them aloud, quietly, and Rayan heard her and frowned, and Yannick leaned over her shoulder. Somewhere behind the bowl a chain-link gate clanged shut, and the last boarder pushed past them toward the road, wheels hissing on the pavement.

"Try it as a conversion," Anais said. "Like inches and centimetres. Same length, different units." She wasn't sure it was that simple. Physics had tricked her before with things that looked equivalent and weren't, like mass and weight, which her younger self had treated as one idea and had been gently corrected about in red pen. But the sameness of the number nagged at her. If the two units measured different things, getting identical answers would be a strange accident, and she had learned, mostly from Ms. Okonkwo's quizzes, that strange accidents deserved suspicion before they deserved belief.

Rayan checked his force calculation again, lips moving. Yannick redid the voltage division. Both arrived, once more, at four thousand, and this time Rayan said, slowly, the way a person tests ice before stepping on it, "So volts per metre and newtons per coulomb are equivalent." Nobody argued. The sentence sat there on the concrete between them, and Anais felt something loosen in her chest, the feeling she got when a problem stopped being a wall and became a door, though she could not have said what was on the other side of it yet.

What stayed with her afterward, walking home with the worksheet folded in her back pocket, was not the answer but the shape of the disagreement. Yannick had thought in potentials, Rayan in forces, and she had needed both of them, plus her own suspicion, to see that the two languages were describing one country. It was an odd comfort. She didn't fully understand why the equivalence held, only that it did, and she decided she could carry the not-knowing a while longer, the way you carry a curbside find home before you've worked out what it is.

At the corner by the bus stop she unfolded the page once more and looked at her two brackets. Then she turned back toward the park, where the floodlights had just come on over the empty bowl.

"Hey," she called to the boys, already fifty metres behind her. "Same problem tomorrow. I want to see if we get it again."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
Edouard set the chicken in the pan the way his mother did, skin down, and watched it sweat. Steam rose off it. After twenty minutes the meat was cooked through and pale as a knuckle, sitting in its own cloudy liquid, and when his father tasted it he said nothing, which was worse than eulogizing some other meal he'd rather have had. Edouard cleared the plates and ran the disposal and decided, quietly, that he would make it again on Friday and that this time it would brown.

The next morning he knocked on Ms. Szabó's door to return the ladder his father had borrowed. She was the neighbor whose cooking he could smell from the sidewalk in summer, dark and savory, nothing like his family's steamed everything. He asked, without planning to, whether she had a book.

"Take the orange one," she said. "The others are anachronistic, measurements like 'a walnut of butter.' The orange one is honest."

He read at the kitchen table with his knee bouncing. Between amino acids and sugars, the book said, there is a reaction that browns food and creates much of its flavor, and it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius. Below that, nothing much happens. He looked at the pan hanging over the stove, the one his mother kept on low so nothing would burn, and understood that nothing would burn because nothing would begin.

He called Blaine, who worked summers at a restaurant.

"Maillard reaction," Blaine said, when Edouard described the page. "That's what it's called. We crank the heat for exactly that."

"So it's not cheating. Turning it up."

"It's the opposite of cheating. It's the whole point."

Edouard's mother worked doubles on Fridays, which was why he had claimed the kitchen, and which was also, he suspected, why his father ate whatever appeared without comment, out of some diplomacy he'd never explained. The provenance of their dinners was a kind of exhaustion, meals designed never to fail, and Edouard had absorbed it without ever choosing it. He was eighteen and leaving in the fall. He wanted one dinner that was not just tolerated.

He dried the chicken pieces with paper towels, laid them out, and turned the burner higher than he ever had, high enough that a drop of water skated across the cast iron and vanished. When the meat hit the pan it made a sound he had never heard in that kitchen, a hiss like something being decided. He stood over it and did not move the pieces, though every instinct told him to fuss with them, and the smell that came up was dark and almost sweet, nothing like steam.

His father came in from the yard and stopped in the doorway. "That's burning."

"It's browning."

"Same thing."

Edouard didn't answer. He was watching the edges of the skin turn the color of varnished wood, and thinking that his father and Ms. Szabó would agree on almost nothing, and that both of them were sure.

In the hall, Edouard's mother turned her key twice, the way she always did, and came in still wearing her name tag. The smell reached her before the light did. For a moment she stood with her coat half off, unable to place it, because it belonged to some other house, some other life where someone had waited for her with a hot pan. She found her son at the stove and her husband at the table with his hands folded, watching the boy the way you watch weather.

"Sit down," Edouard said. He set the platter down and it went on ticking faintly from the heat. His father reached for a piece before the words were fully out.

"Edouard," his mother said.

"It needed to be hotter," he said. "That's all. It just needed to be hotter the whole time."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including those who already have hypertension.
story:
The waiting room of the dental office smelled like mint and old carpet, and Hunter sat beside his father with a magazine about well drilling open on his knee. His father, who drilled water wells for a living, kept glancing at it upside down, correcting him quietly when Hunter mispronounced aquifer, saying it slow, the way you'd say a word you'd earned. They had driven forty minutes for this appointment because it was the only clinic in the county taking new patients before the new year, and Hunter had come along because the truck needed new brake pads and the garage was next door.

When the hygienist called his father back, Hunter followed, mostly because the waiting room television was playing a cooking show whose host laughed at everything, and the laughing felt gratuitous after an hour of it. He did not expect anything. His father sat in the chair, paper bib clipped on, and the hygienist wrapped the cuff around his arm because the office took blood pressure on every patient over forty now, a policy printed on a sign Hunter had read twice without thinking about.

The machine hissed and squeezed. His father winced at it the way he winced at the dentist's probing, tolerantly, the way a man tolerates things done to him by institutions. Then the hygienist frowned at the screen and took it again. The second number, she said, was high. The first one too. She wrote both on a card and said the dentist would talk about it, that it was probably the drive and the coffee, but that the reading was high enough to mention to a doctor.

She left the room to fetch the dentist, and for a minute it was just Hunter and his father and the hum of the chair. Hunter looked at the card. The numbers meant nothing to him except that they had made a professional frown twice, which was enough. His father said it was nothing, said his own father had run high his whole life, said the machine liked to make things dramatic. Hunter said nothing back, but he photographed the card with his phone when his father wasn't looking, and later, in the waiting room again while the dentist drilled a filling, he typed both numbers into his phone.

The internet was careful and unhelpful at once. The numbers were high, that was confirmed in the first line. Below that came a page from something called a health institute, and Hunter read it twice. Regular aerobic exercise, it said, things like brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowered blood pressure in many people, including people who already had hypertension. He looked up hypertension. High blood pressure. The same word the hygienist had circled on the card. He read it a third time, because it said in many people, not in everyone, and that small phrase seemed honest in a way the rest of the internet never was.

Khloe had done a unit on this in her health class last semester, so he texted her from the corner of the waiting room, near the fish tank. She answered between what were clearly her own errands, in fragments. That's called hypertension, she wrote, when it stays high like that. Then: it's not a one-day thing, one reading isn't a diagnosis. Then, after a gap: my mom walks every evening now and her numbers came down. Hunter asked if that was guaranteed. Khloe wrote back, no, nothing is, but it helps a lot of people and the doctor still checks.

The dentist was gentle with the news, gentler than Hunter expected, saying only that the reading should go to their family doctor, that this happened often, that plenty of people brought it down. On the drive home his father was quiet in the way he got when the truck needed a decision made about it. Hunter held the phone in his lap. He thought about the aquifer article, how the water was always down there under the field, whether or not anyone had drilled, and how the drilling only mattered if you did it. He decided not to lecture. He had a fact and no diagnosis, a card and a page, and it seemed to him that saying too much would be worse than saying the right amount.

"Dad," he said, still watching the road. "That thing Khloe told me, about her mom. Regular aerobic exercise, like brisk walking or cycling, most days. It lowers blood pressure for a lot of people, even people who already have hypertension. Not everybody. But a lot."

His father drove a quarter mile before he answered. "You googling my numbers on me now."

"You circled them yourself. On the card. You put it in your shirt pocket like it was a receipt you were going to argue with."

His father laughed at that, one short note, and then the truck went quiet again past the grain elevator. Hunter waited. He did not beseech him, though he wanted to, though he had the words lined up. Instead he said, "I could come with you. Evenings, after the shop closes. There's the loop around the reservoir, it's two miles. We could do it most days and see."

His father's hand moved on the wheel, not adjusting anything, just moving. He reached into his shirt pocket at the stop sign and took out the card with the numbers on it, and looked at it a long moment under the cab light. Then he said, "Most days, you said."

"Most days," Hunter said. "We'd start tomorrow."

His father put the card back in the pocket, checked the mirror, and turned the truck toward the reservoir road, the long way home.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: A zero derivative does not guarantee a maximum or minimum: f(x) = x cubed has derivative zero at x = 0, but its graph keeps rising through that point.
story:
The corner store on Delmore Street had a stool behind the register that Ms. Flores let students use after three, provided they bought something and kept their voices down. Makayla had claimed it since September with a bag of friable oatmeal cookies and her calculus workbook open to chapter four, because the credit exam was in eleven days and her mother had already told two aunts she was taking it.

Allison wanted the stool tonight, or rather wanted what came with it. She was scheduled until seven and had a date at six, and she slid a twenty across the counter before Makayla even sat down. "Watch the register, watch the delivery guy, don't let anyone vilify you when the card reader stalls. It stalls."

"You want me to run the store."

"I want you to sit in a chair and press buttons. Ms. Flores already said it's fine. She's in the back doing the order."

Makayla took the twenty, mostly because the store was quiet and the overhead fluorescent hummed at a pitch she could study through. Charles came in at four with his own workbook, having heard from Allison that Makayla was ahead of him, and he set up on the ice cream freezer like it was a seminar table. He was the one who claimed to have derivatives beaten. "You find where the derivative is zero," he said, tapping his pen, "and that's your maximum. Every time. It's a machine, you just turn the crank."

She had believed the same thing until Tuesday. The practice problem Ms. Flores, of all people, had handed her was to graph f of x equals x cubed first and then take its derivative, in that order, and Makayla had spent twenty minutes refusing because graphing felt like the baby version. Then she'd plotted it, point by point on the graph paper flattened against the cookie rack, and found the trouble. The derivative came out to three x squared, which was zero when x was zero, exactly where the crank said a maximum should be. But the graph went up on the left of zero and kept going up on the right of zero, rising straight through the point like it hadn't been informed. The machine had produced a number that was true and useless at once. A zero derivative did not guarantee anything; you had to look.

"Try it," she said now, turning the workbook toward Charles. "Graph x cubed, then set the derivative equal to zero."

"That's backwards."

"It's the whole point. You get zero at zero, and the graph just keeps rising through that point. It never turns around."

Charles copied the function onto his own paper with the air of a man humoring someone, and while he plotted, the delivery guy arrived with three crates and a clipboard, and the clipboard had a form on it that said INDEMNITY AGREEMENT at the top in a font from some earlier decade. The bottom crate had shifted in the truck and half the crackers inside were crushed to grit. Allison, were she present, would have known the protocol. Makayla read the form twice, signed where the guy pointed, and noted that the store was now protected from claims arising from damaged goods, which seemed to her a system where the crackers lost twice.

Ms. Flores came out, inspected the crate, and decided the grit would go into the topping bin for the ice cream sundaes nobody under forty ordered. Then she looked at the workbook still open beside the register. "You found the cubic," she said. It wasn't a question.

"It lied to me."

"It told you the truth. It just didn't tell you everything." She counted the twenty back into the drawer, minus what Makayla owed for the cookies, and went to the topping bin with a funnel.

Charles had finished graphing by then and was quiet in a way Makayla recognized from herself two nights ago. "So how do you ever know it's a maximum?" he asked.

"You check the other side. Or you graph first and let the picture tell you which kind of point it is." She flipped to her real problem, the one from the exam bank: a polynomial for the profit on the store's coffee depending on price, and the question asked for the maximum. She took the derivative, set it to zero, got x equals two and a half, and this time she graphed it before writing her answer. The curve rose, peaked at two and a half, and fell away on either side, an actual hill, an honest one. She boxed it.

At six-twelve Allison hadn't come back, and at six-fifteen a woman arrived wanting lottery numbers checked, and the card reader stalled exactly as promised, twice, while the woman explained loudly that the machine had never done this before and neither had the girl behind the counter. Makayla ran the card a third time. It went through.

Charles packed up his workbook and stood at the door watching the rain start. "So every zero I've ever found on a test," he said, "might not even be a peak."

"Might not be. Graph it."

He pulled his hood up and went out into it, and Makayla turned the stool back toward the counter, unlocked the register drawer for the next customer, and left her answer boxed on the page where she could see it.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
story:
The hallway of her grandmother's house ran from the front door to the kitchen, thirty feet of dark wood floor and doorways on either side, and no matter how many times Charlotte drew it, it lay flat on the page like a diagram in a fire safety pamphlet. She had come for the whole weekend with her sketchbook and a box of pencils, intending to finish a piece for the school exhibition, and instead she had produced four versions of the same dead corridor. She spread them across the kitchen table while her grandmother boiled the kettle, and they all looked like plans for something rather than pictures of it.

The problem had followed her from art class, where Mr. Visser had circled her hallway in pencil and written "where is this going?" in the margin, which Charlotte had taken first as an insult and then, on the bus home, as a genuine question. Where was it going? It ended at the kitchen, at a door with a china cabinet beside it, but on her page it ended nowhere. It simply stopped at the edge of the paper, as flat as the table it sat on.

Her grandmother set down two cups of tea and looked over her shoulder. "That's the passage," she said. "You've drawn it the way a map would."

"That's the problem," Charlotte said. "It looks like a map."

Her grandmother sipped her tea and said nothing more, which was her way of leaving a door open. Charlotte was circumspect about showing unfinished work, but she slid the drawings over anyway, and her grandmother turned each one slowly, as if the answer might be hiding on the back.

Yash arrived that afternoon, cycling the six miles from town because he had heard about the grandmother's house and wanted to draw the stained glass in the front room. He dropped his bag in the hall, saw the sketches, and pulled a chair up to the table without asking. "It's flat," he said.

"I know it's flat."

"No, I mean, it's flat in a fixable way." He took her ruler and laid it across the first drawing, running it along one edge of the floor in the picture. "Look. Your floor lines are parallel. Real floor lines aren't parallel, not to your eye. They slant toward each other." He drew two quick lines with the ruler, one from each bottom corner, and they met at a point in the middle of the page, out in the blank space where the kitchen door was. Then he did the same with the ceiling lines, and the door frames, and the edges of the rug, and all of them crowded toward that same single point. The hallway sprang backward into the page like a room you could walk into.

Charlotte sat back. She picked the drawing up and held it at arm's length, then close, then at arm's length again. "How did you know to do that?"

"Art history unit," Yash said. "We just did it. Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective. Drawing the lines so they meet at a vanishing point, to show depth on a flat surface. That point, right there." He tapped the place where all her lines crossed. "Everything goes to it."

She spent the rest of the afternoon redoing the drawing, and the strange thing was how it felt less like drawing and more like discovering something that had been in the hallway all along, waiting for her to notice. She kept standing up and walking to the end of the passage and crouching down to see how the floorboards converged, then returning to the table to check whether her eyes were telling the truth. Where should the vanishing point sit? If she moved it left, the whole hallway swiveled as if she had shifted her feet. If she raised it, the ceiling climbed. The drawing wasn't a record of the hall; it was a record of where she stood in it. That idea coagulated slowly in her mind over three cups of tea, until it felt solid enough to act on.

But by evening she was unsettled again, and she knew why. The perspective drawing was more convincing, and yet it was also, in a way, more of a lie. The hallway was full of things perspective ignored: the way the light went amber near the kitchen, the way the far door looked smaller but her grandmother had once carried a wardrobe through it, the way memory made the passage longer than it was. Mr. Visser's question, where is this going, had two answers now. The lines went to a vanishing point. But the drawing itself, what did it want? A convincing illusion, or something truer to how the hallway actually pressed on her when she stood in it at dusk? She liked that the two impulses made a kind of counterpoint, both sounding at once, neither one drowning the other out, and she didn't want to choose yet.

She texted Nora a photo of the finished perspective drawing, then a photo of the flat one, then a photo of the actual hallway, and wrote: which one is more real? Nora replied with three thinking emojis and nothing else, which Nora would defend as a legitimate critical position.

At the kitchen table, under the lamp, Charlotte began a fifth drawing. She drew the vanishing point first, small and deliberate, a point of graphite at the center of the blank page, and then set the ruler against the edge of the paper and whispered, "Okay. Where am I standing?"

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Japan has one of the world's oldest populations, with about 29 percent of its people aged 65 or over in the early 2020s.
story:
"You have forty minutes of highway and then I'm confiscating the phone for the boarding queue," Maelys said from the passenger seat, holding Jayden's phone above her head like a trophy she had no intention of returning. Jayden sat wedged between a cooler and Nikolai in the back of his mother's van, which smelled like sunscreen and the sandwiches nobody had touched yet. They were driving him to the airport for his exchange term in Osaka, and Ms. Joshi, who apparently never slept, had emailed at six that morning: "Your population pyramid analysis was blank. Submit before you board or take the incomplete."

"You submitted a blank page?" Nikolai said, delighted, unwrapping a sandwich purely for the drama of it.

"It wasn't blank. It had my name." Jayden took the phone back and opened the assignment. The pyramid for Japan sat on the screen like a weirdly elegant tree, narrow at the trunk, heavy in the branches. He was supposed to say what the country would need more of in thirty years, schools or nursing homes, and defend it. He had assumed the answer would be obvious. It was not being obvious.

"Okay, so," he said, tilting the screen toward Nikolai. "A pyramid is just age bars stacked up. Wide bottom, lots of kids, you build schools. Wide top, lots of old people, you build, I don't know, ramps." Nikolai leaned over, chewed, and pointed at Japan's shape with a pickle. "That's not a pyramid, that's a wine glass." He was right, unfortunately. The bottom was pinched and the top was swollen, and Jayden read the caption twice because the number seemed to be messing with him.

"Twenty-nine percent," he said. "Twenty-nine percent of everybody in Japan is sixty-five or over. As of the early 2020s." He did the math on the cooler lid with a marker that was mostly dead. "That's like if our whole grade, plus the grade above, plus half the teachers, were all sixty-five plus. It's one of the oldest populations on the planet."

"So the answer is nursing homes," Maelys said, twisting around. "Write nursing homes, hit send, eat a sandwich."

"That's the answer if you only read the top," Jayden said, and she made a face at him, which was fair, because that was exactly the kind of sentence he mocked her for. But the pinched bottom was bothering him. Fewer kids now meant fewer parents later, which meant fewer kids after that, and he tried to sketch it, arrows curling forward through time, a shape unraveling like a sweater. The country would need the nursing homes, yes, and also it would need to keep the schools it had, because the whole epistemology of the thing was that you could not just read one bar. You had to read what every bar was about to become. He did not say "epistemology" out loud. Nikolai would never let him live.

"Wait," Nikolai said, watching the screen over his shoulder. "If it's twenty-nine percent old people, how do the caregivers, like, exist? Who's changing the diapers?" Jayden scrolled and found a line about care workers and immigration and shrugged. "That part I don't know. The pyramid tells you the shape of the pressure, not who lifts it." Maelys said, "That's the most thoughtful thing you've ever said and you're going to fail because you said it instead of typing it," and he shushed her, typing fast.

His mother took the littoral highway exit, the one that ran along the water, and the light came off the harbor and made the screen hard to read, which felt like the universe taking sides against him. He wrote it anyway, in fragments: the glass shape, the twenty-nine percent aged sixty-five or over in the early 2020s, one of the world's oldest, therefore nursing homes first, but schools not abandoned, because the narrow base was a promise about the future and promises about the future deserved ramps too. He wanted to add that he was about to walk into the exact country he was describing, which was either cheating or fieldwork, and he couldn't decide which, so he left it in.

"Ten minutes to the terminal," his mother called, and Maelys reached back to hold his coffee so he could use both thumbs. He hit submit at 63 percent battery, 8 minutes before boarding, and Nikolai read the confirmation aloud in a British accent for no reason anyone could defend. At the curb he hugged his mother, who told him to call when he landed, and Maelys said, "If their whole grade is sixty-five plus, do not make friends with anyone under seventy, you'll be a minority," and Nikolai just handed him the dead marker, a gift for the plane.

At the gate, waiting, he looked up the pyramid for his own city, out of curiosity, and found it sitting there: wide at the bottom, narrow at the top, a shape almost exactly backwards from the one he had just written about. Somewhere between the two, he supposed, was everything that was going to happen to both places. The gate agent called his row. He put the phone in his pocket and got in line.

"Window seat?" the attendant asked.

"Window seat," he said.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, one Frida wears a white European-style Victorian dress and the other wears a traditional Tehuana dress, a contrast often read as her mixed European and Mexican heritage.
story:
Madeline would tell you she came to the studio that Thursday because the critique was due Friday, and that she had known all along which Frida she would write about. Only one of those things was true. The studio occupied the back half of a donated storefront, its windows fogged with kiln dust, and Mr. Nakamura had taped a print of The Two Fridas to the easel by the sink where he kept his coffee, as if the painting were a student who had arrived early.

"You have to pick the left one," Danae said, dropping her bag on the splattered table. "The one in the white dress. She's holding the scissors. She's the one doing something."

Anthony leaned against the stool he never actually sat on. "The right one's the real Frida. She's got the little portrait of Diego on her heart, and her vein's still connected. That's her actual life. The other one is bleeding out into nothing."

"Both of them have her face," Madeline said, and immediately regretted it, because it sounded like the kind of thing Mr. Nakamura said when he wanted them to slow down.

She had been assigned the painting two weeks ago, a formal analysis, colour and composition and symbolism, the vocabulary listed on the handout like ingredients for a recipe she didn't know how to cook. She had put it off, then put it off again, and told her mother she was "working on it," which had felt true at the time and was not. What she had actually done was stare at the image on her phone at eleven at night, deciding that the white Frida was the true one because white was the dominant note, because the dress filled more of the canvas, because the bleeding arm forced your eye there first. She had half a page written to prove it.

Danae pulled the print off the easel and laid it flat under the clip lights. "Look at the dress on the right. It's not just colourful, it's a whole different kind of clothing. That's a Tehuana dress. Traditional Mexican. My grandmother had one for Day of the Dead, not the same, but the kind of thing."

"The left is Victorian," Anthony said, surprising all of them, including himself. "I looked it up for my piece. European, corseted, all that white. My tutor called it Victorian and I wrote it down because it sounded like it mattered."

"It does matter," Madeline heard herself say, and something assembled itself in her head with an almost audible click, the way a door you'd been pushing finally turns out to pull. Two women, one face, one dress from Europe and one from Mexico, seated on a bench holding hands in a storm-colored waste. It was not two Fridas arguing about which one got to be real. It was one woman sitting with both halves of where she came from, and the heart in the European Frida had been cut, and the heart in the Tehuana Frida still beat with the little portrait pinned to it, and Madeline's half-page of "dominant colour" suddenly looked like it had been written by someone who hadn't looked at the painting at all.

"Fine," Danae said, "but if you had to say which one is the real one."

"That's the wrong question. Or it's a question the painting is asking on purpose and refusing to answer."

Mr. Nakamura had drifted over, mug in hand, the way he did when an argument had gotten good enough to leave alone. He said nothing, which Madeline understood now was a kind of teaching, though at the time it felt like complicity, the silence of an adult who could fix your mistake and chose to let you find it yourself, or find out you'd already made it.

She sat down with her draft. The first paragraph, she saw, had been a lie told confidently, the kind of impermeable sentence that lets no doubt in and therefore no truth either: the white Frida dominates and therefore is the subject. She crossed it out. In its place she wrote that the composition held the two figures in deliberate symmetry, the joined hands and the shared vein forming the horizontal axis, and that the sky's grey flatness seemed to presage nothing so much as the storm inside the bodies, though she would have to fix that sentence later, since the painting already knew the storm and wasn't waiting for it. She wrote for forty minutes while Danae and Anthony argued about scissors and Diego at the other table, their voices rising and settling like weather.

What she could not resolve, and wrote that she could not, was whether the storm clouds and the exposed hearts made the doubled self a wound or a marriage. She read the paragraph over twice and could not tell if it was honest or just well hedged, and she thought of the half-page she'd written before, how certain it had been, how wrong.

She turned back to the print under the lights and touched the edge of the white dress with one finger, careful not to smudge the glossy surface.

"So which do I hand in," she said, mostly to herself, "the certainty or the question."

"Hand in the question," Anthony said. "It's longer."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Readers usually detect an unreliable narrator through contradictions, such as other characters' words or the events themselves not matching what the narrator claims.
story:
Nevaeh had promised herself she would finish the novel before the weekend ended, but her grandmother's porch had other plans. The wicker chair swallowed her whole, the ice tea sweated rings onto the armrest, and every few minutes someone inside the screen door offered pie, or bug spray, or the opinion that reading in this heat would ruin her eyes. The book in her lap, a slim paperback about a governess who insists the house she works in is haunted, was due to become the first assignment of her first college course, and Ms. Becker had warned them in the last week of high school that the professor would smell an unearned opinion from across the room.

"You're doing that thing," her grandmother said, coming out with a slice of pie Nevaeh had not asked for and would eat anyway. "That thing where you read the same page nine times."

"It's the same paragraph, actually. She says the children adore her, but the little boy keeps trying to send her away. I'm trying to figure out if I'm supposed to believe her."

Her grandmother settled into the other chair with the gravity of a woman who considered porches her professional domain. "In my day we believed governesses and that was that."

"That's because in your day the narrators were reliable." Nevaeh flipped back to chapter six, where she had bent the corner of a page so violently it had nearly torn. She had started marking her copy the way Adriel had shown her back in April, in the library during their free period, when the two of them had spread their books across the table like generals planning a small war. Adriel, who had already taken a semester course through some online program, had leaned over and tapped the margin. "You find them through contradictions," Adriel had said, tapping each spot where another character said something that didn't line up with the narrator's version, or where an event played out differently than the narrator had claimed it would. "Where other people's words, or what actually happens, doesn't match what the narrator says. That's how readers usually catch one." Nevaeh had thought it sounded too easy. It was not too easy. It was, if anything, worse than too easy, because once she started she could not stop, and every book she read afterward turned into a crime scene.

So now the governess's house was a crime scene too. Nevaeh dug a pen out of the porch cushion's depths and began again from the top, bracketing every place where the housekeeper's politeness contradicted the governess's certainty that they shared a terrible secret, every place where a letter arrived, or did not arrive, in a way the governess had insisted was impossible. The pattern emerged slowly, like a photograph developing. The governess claimed to be the only adult protecting the children. The housekeeper, in her mild and careful elocution, kept arranging for the children to be sent away from the governess. The governess claimed the little girl had spoken to a ghost. The little girl, asked directly, asked to go to school instead. Somewhere around the twelfth bracket, Nevaeh felt the small, absurd exhilaration of a person catching a stranger in a lie after two hundred pages of taking that stranger at her word.

"There you go again," her grandmother said. "Doing the face."

"What face?"

"The one your mother makes when she's winning an argument with a receipt."

Nevaeh laughed, which nearly cost her the pen down between the cushions. She explained, as best she could without giving the whole plot away, because her grandmother had a policy of wanting to read anything Nevaeh liked, that the whole book might be an invention, that the ghosts might only exist in the governess's telling, and that the author had built it so no one inside the story could ever check. Her grandmother considered this while eating pie in small, judicial bites.

"So the woman lying to the children is telling the story," her grandmother said slowly. "And we only have her word."

"That's the trap. Except it's not a trap exactly, because you can catch her. You just have to watch where the other people and the actual events stop agreeing with her."

"And then what. Then you know the truth?"

Nevaeh opened her mouth and found she did not have anything confident to put in it. Because that was the part her inchoate notes, three pages of them in the back of the paperback, kept circling without landing on. She knew the governess's account failed to match what others said and what happened, and she knew that meant the reader should not trust it. Whether that made the governess mad, or deceptive, or simply desperate to matter in a house where no one had asked her opinion, the book would not say. Maybe, she thought, the point was the watching itself, the reader standing at the window of the narrator's mind, unable to leave, unable to fully believe.

"Maybe not the whole truth," she said at last. "Maybe just the lie."

Her grandmother nodded as though this were a perfectly ordinary thing to conclude about a person, and went inside for more ice. Nevaeh looked at her bristling page of brackets, at the governess's serene final paragraph claiming all had been vindicated, and then, on the inside of the back cover, wrote one line to herself: not what happened, but what can't be trusted. She underlined it twice, then, feeling that even that was too certain, added a small question mark and closed the book as the first fireflies came up from the lawn.
